items.how: Starred explain question (6 marks, level of response): paramecia in pond water, solution A and solution B; graphs show the mean number of contractile vacuole pumps per 30 s against time; explain the results using the graphs.
items.ms: Level of response: Level 1 describes the graphs with reference to osmosis (water potential gradient); Level 2 compares solutions A and B with pond water or the cytoplasm; Level 3 explains the graphs. items.how: Very high blood cholesterol alters HDL structure, making it less effective; diagram of HDL and altered HDL (ApoA-1, phospholipid layer, CE, PC, ApoM, RBP4, CRABP1): (i) compare and contrast the structure of HDL with altered HDL (3). items.name: Genetic diversity of reintroduced Scottish beavers

items.name: Mating strategies, reproductive success and genetic diversity
items.how: 6-mark level-of-response (marked *): three mating strategies are described (sperm with a longer middle region, with a graph of middle region length against swimming speed, in females mating with many males; zebra longwing butterfly spermatophores containing sperm and nutrients plus chemicals that make the female less attractive to other males; eastern box turtle females mating with many males and storing sperm for years). Comment on the effect of the strategies on the reproductive success of males and females and on the genetic diversity of offspring.
items.ms: Level of response using basic information (I), reproductive success (R) and genetic diversity (G) per strategy. Longer middle region: faster swimming (more mitochondria supply ATP), better chance of fertilising for that male, selection pressure, more offspring with the same father so possibly less diversity, though many males and eggs could raise diversity. Spermatophore: sperm plus nutrients for more or better eggs, chemicals reduce other males mating, more offspring from the same father so less diversity. Sperm storage: offspring without a mate, more success for the female and the males that mated, offspring with different fathers so more diversity, though not mating with new males each year could reduce it. 1-2 marks for basic information or R or G for one or two strategies; 3-4 for three or four R or G points; 5-6 for R and G across all (or most) strategies.

items.name: Evolution of honeycreepers from common ancestor
items.how: Six-mark level-of-response Explain (starred) of how two honeycreeper species could have evolved from a common ancestor, using the table of habitat, population, food source and island distribution plus own knowledge.
items.ms: Level of response, 6 marks. Generic speciation: ancestor on the islands / shorter or less powerful beak; colonisation of a new island / geographical isolation; changed environment, competition for food, new selection pressures; genetic variation or mutation giving new alleles; advantageous alleles give survival and reproduction and are passed on; repeated over many generations to a new species; reproductive isolation. Amakihi: longer beak to drink nectar/sap or reach spiders and insects; larger population as it can use more habitats and foods. Palila: more powerful beak to crack seed coats; eats seeds and berries. L1 (1-2): basic generic account, or detailed generic plus a basic link to one species; L2 (3-4): L1 plus linkage to one or both species (basic for one = 3, detailed for one or basic for both = 4); L3 (5-6): detailed for one and basic for the other = 5, detailed for both = 6.

items.name: Frozen sperm in breeding programmes: pros and cons
items.how: Six-mark level-of-response Discuss (starred) of the advantages and disadvantages of using frozen sperm in breeding programmes for the endangered Akhal-Teke and Caspian horse breeds, using a table comparing fresh with frozen and thawed sperm (percentage that can swim, survival time, percentage with damaged DNA) and a graph of successful pregnancies against percentage of sperm that can swim (r = +0.90).
items.ms: Level of response, 6 marks. Data: fresh sperm has more swimmers, longer survival and less DNA damage than frozen and thawed sperm (quantitative comparison, e.g. double in fresh, 59% decrease in survival); positive correlation, and r = +0.90 is a strong positive correlation. Advantages: samples from many males, captive and wild, even dead males; artificial insemination or IVF to raise numbers and avoid extinction; selecting samples to maintain genetic diversity and prevent inbreeding; frozen sperm takes little space and stores for a long time. Disadvantages: lower fertilisation and pregnancy success (poorer swimming, shorter survival); damaged DNA or mutations causing failed fertilisation, embryos not developing, miscarriage or genetic disease; cost of equipment, specialist staff and storage; needs females of breeding age. L1 (1-2): isolated generalised points; L2 (3-4): some linkage and structure; L3 (5-6): sustained, well-structured reasoning.
